newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel economic slowdown continues in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Israel economic slowdown continues in 1997.

text.p: A slowdown in Israel's economic growth, which started in early 1996, continued in the first half of this year, the Bank of Israel said on Wednesday.
The central bank said the slowdown was accompanied by a continued increase in unemployment but was offset by improving trends in inflation and the balance of payment deficit.
Per capita private consumption stabilised, while overall investment declined in the first half of the year.

The bank said these trends stemmed from an ending of the effect of the early 1990s immigration wave, the ebbing of the positive atmosphere created by the Middle East peace process and continuing tight fiscal and monetary policy.

Inflation was an annual 10.2 percent in the first half of the year, slightly higher than the upper government target of 10 percent. But inflation expectations remained within the government target of seven to 10 percent in 1997, the bank said.

Foreign currency inflows reached record levels, particularly in the private sector. Towards the end of the half year demand for foreign currency grew after the government instituted a change in the exchange rate mechanism in mid-June.
The Bank of Israel said it had purchased $7 billion of foreign currency to ensure that the shekel remained within its trading bands.
Activity in the construction sector declined in the half while there was a slight increase in demand in retail trade and bank credit.
In the first quarter gross domestic product and industrial production rose slightly, compared with the first quarter of 1996.
The trend of rapid improvement in Israel's trade deficit, which began in early 1996, slowed significantly this year.
Real-term wages rose some 0.5 percent in comparison with the first quarter of 1996, particularly in the business sector, the central bank said.
In the first five months the government budget was in surplus but this was wiped out by a particularly high deficit in June.
The overall deficit is largely due to a shortfall in government revenues but this has been offset to some extent by an unexpected decline in expenditure, the central bank said.
In the six months the central bank reduced its effective key lending rate from 16 percent to about 14 percent.
